lessons.title: Start with the most forcing moves and list every capture
lessons.text: When a position offers many options, work through them one at a time, beginning with checks and captures. In tactical puzzles make yourself list every capture, not only the obvious one, and split a hard position into smaller tasks. If the enemy king is weak, captures near it deserve the first look.

lessons.title: Scan for loose pieces first
lessons.text: Most tactics, whether forks, pins or skewers, start with an undefended piece, especially when a king is exposed. Make it the first thing you check, for both sides. A piece with a single defender still counts as loose, and a defended pawn can still be won if it is attacked more times than it is guarded. Forgetting that something hangs at the end of a line is a very common calculation error.

lessons.title: Scan the whole board, including quiet pieces
lessons.text: Tunnel vision causes a large share of club blunders. A player sees his own attack and misses the queen about to be taken, or his brain filters out a rook that looks harmless but decides the puzzle. Before you commit, check every piece and the other side of the board. A piece far from the action often holds the key to the combination.

lessons.text: Name the opponent's main plan, the square or piece he is heading for and the direction the danger comes from before you pick a move. A quiet move that disrupts that plan is often better than a flashy one of your own.

lessons.title: Check what the opponent threatens before every move
lessons.text: Run a quick check for the reply that hurts: a rook move that leaves a back-rank threat, a check you assumed was mate but can be blocked, or a tempting capture that leaves your queen stuck guarding against mate. Many attacks fail because one counter-threat was never looked at. In a mutual attack, the side that takes a foot off the gas can be mated first.

lessons.title: Find the opponent's best defence before relying on a check
lessons.text: A check can be met by moving the king, capturing the checking piece or blocking, and club players often forget the block. Before committing to a tactic, work out the opponent's strongest reply rather than the one you are hoping for. A combination only counts if it survives that reply.

lessons.title: Check every recapture the opponent has
lessons.text: In a run of captures it is easy to take the wrong piece, or to assume the opponent must recapture one way when a pawn recapture changes everything. Before you capture, write down each way he can take back and what each leaves hanging. A quick count prevents a common blunder in which a piece is lost to a recapture you did not consider.

lessons.title: Calculate the whole line once mate is close
lessons.text: When mate is near, instinct offers several equally tempting checks, and only a fully calculated line shows which one works. Move order matters because the wrong check can hand the king an extra square. Multi-move mate puzzles are good practice for exactly this.

lessons.title: Ask what happens if you play it anyway
lessons.text: A move that looks impossible, because it drops a piece or seems to run into a refutation, is often playable once you test it. Calculate the concrete line before you rule it out, and let yourself look at moves you dismissed by reflex. Finding creative ideas depends more on being willing to look than on calculating harder.

lessons.title: Give a failed line fifteen more seconds
lessons.text: When a move you badly want to play seems to fail, do not drop it at the first refutation. Stay on the final position for about fifteen seconds, because the extra look often turns up a check or a pin that rescues the idea. Keep this for lines that matter, not every variation.

lessons.title: Keep calculating after the line seems to end
lessons.text: Many calculation errors come from stopping a variation one move too early, often right after a capture or a quiet retreat. Take each important line one move further and ask what the opponent still has. This matters most in lines you are hoping will work, because the extra move is where traps and trapped pieces show up.

lessons.text: A move you rejected earlier may work now because the king has stepped aside, a defender has gone or a file has opened. Ask the question again on each move. In long variations, take captured pieces off your mental board so you do not assume a square is still guarded.

lessons.title: Judge by concrete lines, not by how a move looks
lessons.text: A lead in development, a tidy structure or a natural-looking move does not justify a decision unless a specific line backs it up. Test your first impression with a variation, and look one move deeper than the obvious capture or threat. Keep questioning your assumptions, because apparent threats and apparent advantages are often illusions.

lessons.title: Treat standard rules as guides and let concrete lines decide
lessons.text: Positional rules and textbook tactics support calculation and never replace it. Breaking a principle is fine when the specifics justify it, for example giving up a good knight, putting a pawn in front of your king or leaving the standard pattern, and a textbook idea can fail in the actual position. From about 1500 up, expect to override general rules regularly.

lessons.title: Look for a better move before playing the good one
lessons.text: Even when a good move is staring at you, take three to five seconds to ask whether something cleaner or stronger exists. Strong players treat their first idea as a draft and look for ways to optimise it. Routine developing moves and rook moves played on autopilot are where easy improvements get missed.

lessons.title: Handle the most urgent thing first
lessons.text: When several moves look good, play first the one that exploits or removes the most temporary factor, such as stopping the opponent castling before improving a piece. When defending against a stream of threats, work out which cannot wait and choose the least ugly answer.

lessons.title: Check the small details a tactic depends on
lessons.text: A combination works only if specific conditions hold, such as a rook being undefended, a flight square being covered or a pawn standing on a particular square. Verify each one before committing. Do not assume a pattern that worked in another game works here.

lessons.title: Build intuition through pattern recognition
lessons.text: Fast, confident moves come from stored patterns, and patterns come from solving many tactics and studying instructive games. Once a pattern is familiar, you can see that a position is winning without finding the exact mate, and you accept that judgement call. Back the instinct with a short check of the forcing lines.

lessons.title: Look for in-between moves, ideally with tempo
lessons.text: Before making the obvious capture or retreat, ask whether an intermediate move first removes the annoying threats. The best ones carry a threat of their own, so the opponent cannot fix the original problem. When you are the one under attack and see no direct answer, look for a flaw in the opponent's last move.

lessons.title: Do not play a move just because it attacks something
lessons.text: A threat does not make a move good, since the attacked piece can often just step away and you have gained nothing. Beginners love checks and attacks on pieces, so ask what purpose the move serves. Resist the urge to hit the queen straight away if improving a piece does more.

lessons.title: Prefer moves that do two jobs
lessons.text: Prefer the move that defends, develops and connects pieces at the same time over a single-purpose one. A queen move that guards a pawn and links the rooks beats a rook move that only defends. A developing move that also carries a threat is better still.

lessons.title: Recheck your first-move candidates before going deep
lessons.text: Long variations often fall apart because a better first move was never on the list, and the opponent finds it at the board. Before sinking time into a deep line, run through the candidates at move one again. Expect most of what you calculate never to appear in the game, since the work still sharpens your judgement.

lessons.title: Break chaotic positions into plain facts
lessons.text: Complicated positions are usually four or five separate concrete facts stacked together, such as what hangs, who is ahead in material and how many defenders each piece has. List them one at a time instead of tuning out. Learning to embrace messy positions is one of the quickest ways to improve.

lessons.title: Compare two candidate moves side by side
lessons.text: When two moves or two positions look alike, find the specific difference between them instead of judging each on its own. With two similar checks, work through one, then see how the other fixes its problem. A more advanced version holds both versions in mind at once and waits for the lines to diverge.

lessons.title: Count attackers and defenders, then check what the capture costs
lessons.text: Numbers matter, but so do details: a pinned piece is not a real defender, and a capture that loses your queen is not a real attack. A pawn with more attackers than defenders can also be safe if taking it wrecks the capturer's structure. Work out what each capture actually leads to before trusting the count.

lessons.title: Check what each pawn move weakens or releases
lessons.text: Every pawn move leaves something behind: a square it no longer guards, a piece that lost its support, a diagonal that has opened. After an opponent's pawn move, list which pieces are now undefended and which squares are weaker. Do the same for your own pawn moves before you play them, since a push can hand an enemy knight an outpost or give a tactic a place to land.

lessons.title: Look for forkable squares and aligned pieces
lessons.text: Check whether the enemy king and queen, or queen and rook, stand on squares a knight can hit together, or on one line a bishop or rook can use. If the fork is not there yet, look for the preparatory move, such as a bishop move that clears the knight's route, or a move that attacks a piece and sets up the fork next. Know your own fork squares too, so you do not walk into them.

lessons.text: Good candidate moves come from putting several small facts together. An uncastled king, an open centre and a queen on an exposed square point toward a tactic, and so does an undefended rook sitting behind an x-ray. Make it a habit to ask where the opponent's queen is, because the queen attracts more tactics than any other piece.

lessons.text: You do not need to see every line to the end. Once you know the key refutation fails, or you can see a clear way to meet the last threat, stop and play. lessons.title: Finish development before you attack
lessons.text: Even with an edge or an extra piece, bring everything into play before launching an attack or pushing flank pawns. Pushing a big central or wing pawn before your queenside is developed is biting off more than you can chew. An opponent who leaves pieces at home can lose in a handful of moves.

lessons.title: Develop before you grab pawns
lessons.text: Do not rush to take a pawn while your king is in the centre and your pieces are still at home. Finishing development and castling is usually worth more than a pawn, and an opponent who is far behind can be punished by developing and opening the centre. Most quick wins come from following the basic principles and noticing the tactics they create.

lessons.title: Develop pieces before worrying about pawn structure
lessons.text: In the opening, speed of development matters more than small structural flaws such as doubled pawns. Choose recaptures that bring a piece into play, and do not spend a move on a pawn when a piece is still at home. If you get ahead in development, use it quickly, because slow moves let the opponent catch up and the initiative fades.

lessons.text: A lead in development is temporary, so cash it in with a central pawn break before he catches up. Opening lines when you have more pieces in play gives them targets and makes tactics work. An awkwardly placed enemy queen is a sign to look for this.

lessons.title: Meet a flank attack with a strike in the centre
lessons.text: When the opponent starts a wing attack before finishing development, answer by opening the centre. A flank attack tends to leave the centre underprotected, and opening it exposes the lack of development. The same applies when the opponent spends many moves shuffling on one side: strike in the middle.

lessons.title: Master simple principled chess before exotic theory
lessons.text: Classical, principled openings teach how to develop, fight for the centre and coordinate pieces, and those basics are hard to see when buried under theory. Set-ups that give the opponent the centre or demand exact move orders, such as the Pirc or the Scandinavian, suit players who already have the basics, around 1600 or 1700 and up. Simple chess done well is the base that later styles need.

lessons.title: Learn the opening rules, then spot when to break them
lessons.text: Principles such as develop first and keep the pawns around your king still are defaults. They give way to concrete play, for example when a direct pile-up on a weakness works, or when the opponent is already ignoring them. If he plays pawn moves instead of developing, you earn the right to take liberties. Knowing the rule well is what lets you recognise the exception.

A compact, practical repertoire also wins games quickly for players short of study time.

Castle when it suits your plan.

lessons.title: Avoid moving the same piece repeatedly in the opening
lessons.text: Every extra move with one piece is a lost tempo. Trading a piece that has moved three times for one that has moved once costs two moves, and an early trade that wrecks your own structure compounds the damage. Count the tempi before agreeing to such an exchange.

lessons.title: Do not combine e6 and g6 in Sicilian structures
lessons.text: Playing both e6 and g6 in Sicilian-type positions leaves d6 and the dark squares weak, and a white knight landing on d6 is very hard to dislodge. In most positions the pairing is a mistake, so choose one of them or find another setup unless a concrete line supports it. Treat it as a strong default with a few exceptions.

lessons.title: Borrow ideas from openings you do not play
lessons.text: Openings share principles in the way languages share roots. When you see a game in an opening you do not play, engage with it instead of closing the tab, because its ideas can be applied to your own repertoire. You do not need to play an opening to learn from it.

lessons.title: Catalogue the typical pawn structures of your openings
lessons.text: Learn the pawn structures that arise from your openings and the plans that go with them. Structure is not the most important feature of a position, yet knowing the standard plans lifts your opening understanding at intermediate level and above. Think of each opening in terms of its structures.

lessons.title: Face the area of chess you avoid
lessons.text: If you are weak at attacking, endgames or openings, force yourself into those positions instead of dodging them. Avoiding an area for years leaves long-term weaknesses, and opponents rated a few hundred points higher will have far more experience there. Facing the weakness is the only way it gets better.

lessons.title: Practise visualisation by calculating without moving pieces
lessons.text: Calculate lines in your head, using arrows or a board only to check, because long-line visualisation is the main skill behind finding tactics. Pawn races and pawn endings are easy places to start. Follow along even when it is hard, since the effort stretches your ability.

lessons.text: When your answer to a puzzle is wrong, find out what drew you to it. The attraction shows what you overvalue or take for granted. lessons.title: Treat won positions as practice for precision
lessons.text: A clearly winning position carries little risk, so use it to practise good habits: improve your position, pick up pawns cleanly and remove nuisances in a sensible order. Those habits carry over into harder games. Winning positions can still go wrong if you relax.

lessons.title: Read chess books with a purpose
lessons.text: No single book carries you to the next level, so do not read to tick a box: know why you opened it and engage with it. Positional books are best taken slowly, and books packed with well-explained examples are the most useful, since the more games you take in the better. For club players he recommends Grooten's Chess Strategy for Club Players, and also Improve Your Chess Pattern Recognition.

lessons.title: Accept long-term compensation when you give up material
lessons.text: Gambit players must be comfortable without a quick mate. Compensation can be long term, in the form of weak squares or a king that stays unsafe even after castling, so be ready to play a pawn or two down on those lasting trumps. Know which kind you have, though: if the opponent is about to castle out of it, your time to use the compensation is short. You can also give a pawn back if it forces an awkward set-up.

If White carries on with g5, Black plays ...d4 and, after gxf6, recaptures with the bishop and stands better. Qd2 is White's sensible move, so this is a trap to watch for against unprepared opponents.

dragon.text: In the Accelerated Dragon, develop ...Nf6 and castle before committing the d-pawn. An early ...d6 lets White transpose into a main-line Dragon with f3, while waiting keeps ...d5 available as a single strike. Push ...d5 only after castling short, because earlier it runs into Bb5, pinning the c6 knight and threatening Nxc6 followed by Bxc6, which forks king and rook.

dragon.text: If White plays Dragon-style moves against the Accelerated move order, Black profits from not having played ...d6. After f3 and Qd2 the break ...d5 comes in one go, a tempo better than the same position in the main-line Dragon. Against Bc4, castle and then play ...Qb6 to set up ...Nxd4, because the bishop on e3 is unprotected (an immediate ...Nxd4 just loses a piece, and this is the trap Fischer once fell into against Panno).

dragon.text: Treat ...g6 combined with ...e6 as a near-absolute no in the Accelerated Dragon. It leaves d6 and the dark squares around it badly weakened, and White's knight punishes that quickly (in his own example Nb5 and a queen fork on c7 won material). The many pawn moves this setup needs are fine, as long as the pieces keep developing and that pairing is avoided.

Play ...Nf6 before ...Bg7: if White takes on c6 and pushes e5, ...Qa5+ wins that pawn.

carokann.text: In the Tartakower line (after Nd2, ...dxe4, Nxe4, ...Nf6, Nxf6+) recapture with ...exf6, not ...gxf6. Black accepts a damaged structure in return for easy development: the bishop goes to d6, then ...Bg4 ties down a white knight on f3, and White must either weaken with h3 and g4 or retreat the bishop to e2 passively. Do not pick a line only because it leads to one appealing position, since you also need a plan against White's other options, above all the Advance.

pirc.text: The Pirc is the King's Indian setup played against 1.e4, with White's c-pawn still on c2. It has never been refuted and is perfectly playable at club level, but strong players avoid it because White has several good set-ups: the Austrian Attack (f4), the Be3 and f3 English-style attack, and the calm Classical with Be2.

london.text: Black's ...c5 with ...Qb6 is the standard way to unsettle the London, because the early bishop leaves b2 loose. The automatic b3 costs a lot (it permanently weakens the dark squares c3, b4 and a3, and b3 combined with c3 is an awkward structure), yet most players who have not prepared drift into it. The accurate answers are hard to find over the board, so learn them in advance; in the Jobava version Nc3 works because Qxb2 runs into Nb5.

Hold off committing the queenside knight and bishop until you see Black's set-up. He adds that a4, stopping ...b5 outright, has lately become more popular than recapturing on c4 with the queen, and Black has struggled to equalise against it.

grunfeld.text: Activity is the point of the Grünfeld: you give White the centre, so be ready to part with the c- or e-pawn early if it keeps your pieces active, and if you would rather play passively, play a Queen's Gambit Declined instead. When a pawn is lost anyway, give it up in the way that does most damage to White's structure (he shows a push that leaves White with an isolated a-pawn) and then hit the centre at once with ...c5.

grunfeld.text: The g7 bishop is Black's key piece, so White works to remove it: Bh6 to trade it (especially once ...h5 has loosened the dark squares) or the d5 exchange sacrifice to uproot it. He says removing the Grünfeld bishop is almost always good for White, so avoid loosening the king's dark squares casually and look to keep the bishop.

grunfeld.text: In the exchange Grünfeld Black's counterplay is speed: ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Bg4 go straight at d4. White's standard answer is Ne2, so that ...Bg4 can be met by f3. In the main line Black's knight usually heads for a5 rather than e5 (f4 would gain White a tempo), and from a5 it can jump to c4.

dutch.text: Be careful with the Bg5 sideline. Chasing the bishop with ...h6 and ...g5 can lose quickly: White retreats Bh4, meets ...g5 with Bg3, and after ...f4 plays e3, so grabbing the bishop allows Qh5 and mate on the h5-e8 diagonal. He also thinks an old book recommendation of ...h6 here is a mistake, because White has strong central strikes such as e4.

benoni.text: From White's side, the standard plan against Benoni structures is to reroute the knight f3, d2, c4 to hit the d6 pawn, a permanent weakness that is hard to remove, and to meet ...a6 with a4 so Black never gets ...b5. Knowing this tells Black to look for counterplay before the knight lands.

benoni.text: Black's main queenside counterplay in Benoni structures is ...a6 and ...b5, often after developing the bishop to d7, which is exactly why White tries to stop it with a4. Another typical resource is to stop White's e5 counterstrike by routing a knight via g4 to e5.

benoni.text: He rates the Benoni structure as objectively favouring White (the engine shows a significant edge), yet says Black's play is easy in practice, which is why the opening has survived for decades. He also likes it as training, since Benoni and Grünfeld positions teach piece coordination and the value of active pieces.
